speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we were dealing with item No. 14 last evening, but the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) finds it necessary to leave this afternoon and he has some remarks he would like to make on item No. 12. I suggest that we revert to this item.
519o2-190i
Marketing services-Marketing of agricultural products including temporary appointments that may be required to be made notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act, the amount available for such appointments not to exceed $50,000, $200,000.

Mr. Chairman, I hasten first to thank the minister for his courtesy in this matter. I appreciate his action in permitting me to speak at this time. I rise to offer to the minister and to the government what I feel are one or two constructive suggestions. It is not my purpose during the course of the remarks I shall make either to criticize or to condemn. I am seized with the feeling that the position of agriculture in this country is of such vital importance to the dominion as a whole that every possible assistance should be given to the farmer, in connection with both the production and the distribution of his products at fair and reasonable market prices. It will be impossible in the time at my disposal to cover the subject with anything like completeness, and accordingly my remarks will of necessity be confined to one or two of the major points in the case. I am sure the minister will appreciate that I am addressing this committee fully conscious of the fact that what I may say will be only a small part of the story which should be told, a story which is of vital importance to the dominion.
There are two factors that should be taken into consideration at the commencement of any discussion of Canadian agriculture. The first is that the Canadian farmer is without a peer in the world. He has demonstrated again and again that not only can he produce products of high quality, but that he personally possesses the characteristics which tend to build up the back-bone of a nation. He has faced, as has his fellow Canadian, the industrial worker, the most difficult and trying of times. He has maintained his equilibrium in the face of extraordinary difficulties and hardships. Not only has he to face, as I said the other day in this 'house, the economic hazards of his high calling, but he is also beset by those factors which have been styled " acts of God " and which are completely beyond his control and the control of those who are responsible for government.
Second,	this	country is fundamentally
agrarian. I have in my hand a record of the 1935 production, both primary and secondary. The primary production for that year was as follows:
Agriculture	$ 622,722,000
Forestry	 227,500,346
Fisheries	 34,427,854
Trapping	- .	8,877,331
Mining	 238,581,268
Electrical	power	 125,123,078

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

In the face of such figures and with the knowledge of the facts of the matter in regard to the importance of agriculture in this country, so readily apparent from these figures, all members of this committee, whether they represent industrial, urban or rural areas, must concern themselves with the problems of the farm, because it is apparent from these figures that agriculture comprises 50 per cent of the primary production of this country. Industrial Canada is directly dependent upon agricultural Canada, and agricultural Canada is directly dependent upon industrial Canada. So we face this whole question, not from any sectional point of view but from that of the loyal and true Canadian.
In December of last year there was released over the signature of the Minister of Agriculture a report which has since become known as the Shaw report. It was a most interesting document prepared by a worthy committee after an investigation of the possibilities of further developing the markets of the United Kingdom for Canada and particularly Canadian agricultural products. Recently, indeed within the week, a further bulletin was released, again over the signature of the hon. minister, which is essentially an illuminated edition of the Shaw report. It is changed slightly here and there, but in the main it embodies a record of the findings of the Shaw committee. I do not wish to repeat here any of the discussions which have been carried on in your committee, Mr. Chairman, within the past week in regard to this new bulletin; I shall deal with it upon its face value and with reference to the factual information that it contains.
This report reminds us that the agricultural activities of Canada are as diversified as it is possible to have them. Within climatic restrictions, the Canadian farmer from Halifax to Victoria engages in the production of all agricultural products. We are wheat farmers, dairy farmers, fruit farmers, potato growers, vegetable growers, truck gardeners and all the rest. However, we have always regarded ourselves primarily as wheat producers. With changing world conditions which have brought about accompanying changes in our wheat markets, with the increase in importance of the dairy production of the eastern provinces, our agrarian picture is indicating a slow- perhaps not so slow-and certain change. Further, extraordinary calamities in western Canada in what have been termed the drought areas have brought all thinking Canadians face to face with the problem of finding a solution of the difficulties which the western farmer, through no fault of his own, has to face, difficulties brought about by two factors,
[Mr. Massty.J
first, the loss of a substantial proportion of his foreign market and, second, a limitation upon his activities as a result of changing climatic and soil conditions. What, then, is the future of the Canadian farmer? What is the future of the western farmer? Yes, and what is the future of the eastern farmer?
Let me deal specifically with three of our important products, Canadian-wide in their production-eggs, butter and bacon.
Let me deal, first, with eggs. In 1935,
24.594.000	Canadian hens produced 223,540,000 dozen eggs at seventeen cents a dozen, to a total value of $37,763,000. Here is a product that is obviously of great importance to the Canadian farmer. It is interesting to note that of these eggs we exported only 1,300,744 dozen, while our domestic production per capita amounted to 22-39 dozen a year. Unquestionably one of the most important markets available to us for this product is that of the United Kingdom; for hon. members well know that Canadian eggs enter the market of the United Kingdom duty free. As one reads through the bulletin to which I have already referred, so recently released by the minister, and turns to page 48, which deals with eggs, one realizes at once that the domestic production of eggs in the United Kingdom is far below their own requirements even though there has been a sharp increase in their production in the past few years; but in spite of this increase we find written in this report at page 48:
On this basis of production home supplies accounted for about three-fifths of the total consumption in 1936, or 38 eggs out of every 62 consumed.
Thus it is that in spite of what has been done in the United Kingdom to increase the production of eggs, only thirty-eight out of every sixty-two eggs consumed there are produced within its boundaries. Then, if we turn to the appendix to the report, at the top of page 77 we find that in 1936 there were
24.653.000	great hundreds of eggs imported into the United Kingdom from many different countries', among which there were as important factors the Irish Free State, Australia. Denmark, Poland and the Netherlands. Of this import of 24,653,000 great hundreds of eggs, Canada exported only 103,000 great hundreds, or 0-4 of one per cent. The minister may say at once that our own domestic requirements run so close to our own production that we have not available for export eggs in any outstanding quantity. But why is it, when we realize that we are such an insignificant factor in the British egg market, that Canadian agriculture cannot take advantage of the fact that the mother country

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
prefers to buy from within the empire if at all possible, especially if the quality of the empire product is equal to that of the product of other countries. On pages 49 and SO of the minister's bulletin there appear the recommendations of the Shaw committe which tell us in part:
1.	Canada's eggs at present are not only sold as a cold storage product, but because of our method of grading are classified as "Grade B" storage.
Further:
2.	It would appear that for a certain part of each year

at least 5 or 6 months-Canada could successfully ship fresh eggs to certain United Kingdom markets.
And further:
3.	The majority of Canadian eggs at present are shipped in crates bearing attractive labels such as "Canadian eggs" but each egg within the case bears the stamp " Empire."
And still further:
Further investigational work should be carried on (possibly by the national research council) in connection with temperature and humidity control during periods of storage and transportation of the product with a view to the elimination of losses due to moulds, spots, etc.
Those are the recommendations of the Shaw report, and there would appear to be no extraordinary difficulty to be overcome. The case is quite clear. We are facing essentially two problems in connection with the export of our eggs to the United Kingdom: (1) We as yet do not produce in volume sufficient to export in large quantities; and (2) such eggs as we do export at the present time are relegated to the limbo of cold storage grade B eggs.
Let me deal now with a second important product, butter. Hon. members must be fully conscious of the subtle and veiled attack that is to-day being made upon the animal kingdom of Canada. It is not going too far to state, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian dairy farmer is in a most hazardous position as a result of the threat, insidious and unrecognized in altogether too many cases, against the dairy cow. The vast and staggering increase in the production of vegetable oils throughout the world is challenging the production of butter in a manner that must not escape the attention of this government, or of any government for that matter. Canada is certainly not in a position at the present time to have her animal kingdom decimated by the vegetable kingdom. One does not wish in any way to impede progress; but in these days when the dairy farmers of Canada are faced with and are facing such extraordinary circumstances, we must regard with extreme seriousness what is
happening in the far corners of the world. I make these remarks by way of introduction to my comments on our butter production.
In 1936 there was produced in Canada a total of both creamery and home made butter of 380,290,500 pounds, of which we exported only 7,697,000 pounds. Our domestic consumption amounted to 340,439,540 pounds, or 31-13 pounds per capita. If we turn to the minister's new bulletin, page 43, we find that the market of the United Kingdom imported no less than the extraordinary amount of 1,092,228,816 pounds of butter from many different countries, chief among which were Australia, New Zealand and Denmark. Canada exported to the United Kingdom in 1936 only 0-42 of one per cent of the total butter imported by Great Britain. The recommendations of the Shaw committee in this connection are also to be found on page 43 and read as follows:
While it appears that Canada's exportable surplus of dairy products to the United Kingdom markets will be for many years in the form of cheese, yet, due to changes in the relative values of cheese and butter in Canada as well as to other influences, it may be necessary during some years to export surplus butter.
Butter makers should continue their efforts to improve the quality of the product, not only on account of the better prices which may be realized for the relatively small quantities which may be exported, but to a greater extent on account of the effect of the export value on the price of the much greater quantity marketed in Canada during periods of export movement.
Again, we must bear in mind that our butter enters the United Kingdom duty free, and that we have here an opportunity to develop this product of our dairy farms for that market; but at the present time, consuming as we do the vast proportion of our own production, we have little surplus butter available for export to any country, let alone the United Kingdom. I fully realize the implication of the recommendations of the Shaw committee when it is stated that for some years to come cheese will be the important export from our dairy industry. Nevertheless we must bear in mind that we are still a negligible factor in a market in which we have free entry and which is certainly available to us.
Against this situation I return to the point I discussed at the beginning of my remarks on butter, and that is the staggering, vast and frightening increase in the world's production of vegetable oils. For example, let us take palm oil. In 1920, in Sumatra, 360 tons were produced; in 1936, 196,996 tons. In the Malay peninsula in 1920 no palm oil at all was produced, but in 1937 42,935 tons were produced. On the west coast of Africa
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

in 1920 there were produced 119,312 tons as against 244,647 tons in 1937. And here, Mr. Chairman, I have taken only one source of vegetable oil, and that is palm oil. For Ceylon, Java and the Philippines, in the production of cocoanut oil a similar story can be told. Let it be remembered that we are continuing to import into Canada increasing quantities of these oils, which in the manufacture of shortening replace lard and butter, and in the manufacture of soap replace animal tallow and grease.
Then consider for a moment the importation of vegetable oil into Canada last year. These figures are as I stated, staggering:

Let me for a moment turn to the production of bacon, the last of the three products I have selected upon which to make a few recommendations to the minister. Canadian bacon is excellent bacon, and the bacon producers of Canada are to be sincerely congratulated on the quality of their product. When it is considered that there is one pig in Canada to every three persons, one can realize how important is our bacon and ham and pork industry.
In discussing this major product, produced in all parts of Canada, we will recall that Canadian bacon enters the United Kingdom duty free, but that we have no tariff preference provided in either of the Canada-United Kingdom trade agreements of 1932 or 1937, although continuance of duty free entrance is assured. Further, the United Kingdom agreements with Canada have assured us of a quota of 2,500,000 hundredweight per annum. As we survey the export figures from 1928 on we realize just how important the United Kingdom market is to the producer of Canadian bacon. In a few moments I shall place upon Hansard the record of our export production, but sufficient be it to say for the moment that from a low in 1931 of 41,595 hundredweight of 112 pounds, our production has increased until in 1937 we exported to the United Kingdom market 1,387,006 hundredweight. But hon. members will note that we have barely passed the halfway mark in our quota.

Again turning to the minister's bulletin, this time to page 28, we will note that whereas Great Britain has in six years more than doubled her domestic production of bacon, nevertheless she is producing only a fraction of her total requirements and is still a substantial customer of many different countries, of which Canada is one. As the Shaw report well reminds us, on page 27 of the minister's bulletin, there is a prejudice against Canadian bacon because immediately after the war much inferior bacon was sold, and this, having been held in storage for some time, seriously damaged the reputation of Canadian bacon.
Let me again remind the committee that the facts of the matter are that whereas we have a quota of 2,500,000 hundredweight against Canadian bacon we have yet only reached the half-way mark in filling that quota. If we turn to pages 33 and 34 of the minister's latest bulletin we shall find a series of recommendations, among which we will read the following:
We feel that action should be taken to develop better merchandising methods. . . .
A careful survey of Canadian bacon as it is handled in the United Kingdom retail shops failed to convince us that it was being merchandised in the best possible manner. On very few occasions was it advertised or sold as Canadian bacon. . . .
Standards of quality must be maintained and improved.
As volume and continuity of supply are essential other efforts will be nullified unless this can be accomplished. . . .
A much higher percentage of sizable Wilt-shires is desirable in Canadian exports. . . .
The grading and selection of Canadian bacon has greatly improved in recent years. . . .
Canadian bacon frequently discolours too quickly after being cut. Necessary investigation to be undertaken to ascertain and remove the cause, if possible. . . .
Now, Mr. Chairman, in what I have said so far I have had a definite purpose in mind. I have considered only three of the important agricultural products of this country-eggs, butter, and bacon; and these I have selected deliberately because of the potential possibilities that they present in the development and advancement of Canadian agriculture. Last summer I spent considerable time in Denmark conducting an extensive and intensive investigation of the methods employed by the government and other agencies for the development of Danish agriculture to its position of great importance in the market of the United Kingdom. The minister realizes as well as if not better than any member of this committee the substantial portion of the British market in eggs, butter and bacon claimed by the farmers of Denmark. Here

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
is a little country of only 17,000 square miles, which means that twenty-four kingdoms of Denmark could be put into the province of Ontario alone. Of Denmark's population of 3,700,000, twenty-three per cent live in one big city in the country, the city of Copenhagen ; thirty-nine per cent live in small towns, and the balance of the population, thirty-eight per cent, live in the country. They are a people completely homogeneous, and of Gotho-Germanic origin, possessed of high character and a deep moral sense, and their honesty is outstanding. Their educational system, as a result principally of the activities of Bishop Grundvik, in the latter part of the nineteenth century, is extraordinarily efficient in the development of the young Dane into full citizenship, with a sense of moral responsibility, not only to his country but to his neighbour.
Let it be remembered that Denmark, as an important factor in the agricultural markets of the world, has been built out of what were virtually the ashes of a country. Disastrous wars with Prussia and Austria had deprived Denmark of her most fertile territories, Schleswig and Holstein, and, further, as a wheat growing country she had lost her markets. Here then in the later half of the nineteenth century was a country that had been soundly defeated by her two archenemies, had lost her most fertile territories, and had been deprived of the outlet for her only major product, wheat. Her people were little more than serfs, lacking both in intelligence and in pride, all of which combined to build down to a nation that was on the verge of disaster. But to-day Denmark, primarily agrarian as she is, is one of the leading agricultural countries of the world, whose products are justly famous for their quality and consumer acceptance. It has been during the last sixty years that she has built herself into a country where 98 per cent of her farmers own their own land; where her agricultural products are of the highest quality and kind; a country in which a new nationalism has sprung up; a country which can boast of a system of social insurance governing sickness, accidents, old age, and all the rest, more widespread than any voluntary system in the world; a country in which only one in a thousand cannot read or write; a country in which there are no immensely rich people or any very poor people. Her farms are not large. There are 204,000 of them in this little kingdom, one-half of which are less than twenty-five acres in size, only twenty-three per cent of them being more than 150 acres. Twenty-nine per cent of her exports to-day
are bacon, meat and other slaughtery products. Her butter, cheese and milk comprise twenty-five per cent of her exports, and eggs eight per cent. Fifty-four per cent of her total exports go to the United Kingdom alone.
If we consider such a country perhaps we are too ready to say that any comparisons between the agricultural development of Denmark and the agricultural development of Canada are too remote to be worthy of the attention that we might give to them. On the contrary, strange though it may seem to say it, the comparison is not so remote as one might at first think.
In Canada there are 729,000 farms; in Denmark there are 204,000. But if we compare the Danish live stock population with the human population, we shall see that their agricultural set-up, if I may so call it, is not so different from our own. In Denmark there is one horse to every six persons; in Canada there is one horse to every four persons. In Denmark there is one head of cattle to every person; in Canada there are four head of cattle to every five persons. In Denmark there is one pig to every person; in Canada there is one pig to every three persons. In Denmark there are seven chickens to every person; in Canada there are five chickens to every person. And yet, keeping in mind that their farms are small and also that many of our farms are vast in area, hon. members will realize from the figures I have given that the Danish set-up for the production of eggs, butter and bacon is not far removed in relative contrast from that of Canada.
But Denmark's approach to her markets in the United Kingdom has been dissimilar to ours. Realizing the position in which she was placed in the latter part of the nineteenth century as a result of the factors I have already mentioned, through governmental agencies she approached the United Kingdom to ascertain the type of product that would be most acceptable in the British market. Note that she did not develop her product and then endeavour to sell it in the United Kingdom; she went first to the United Kingdom and determined the quality and kind of product required, and then went back to her farms to develop that identical product. In this aim she has been most extraordinarily successful. In other words, she realized that the Danish farmer back on his little farm could not possibly know what kind of bacon would be most acceptable to the British market, for example. The government, however, was in a position to find out and to tell him, 'and that is exactly what the government did, with the net result that, realizing that-
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

quality was the only basis upon which she could possibly hope to compete in the market of the United Kingdom, Denmark has developed for that market a product which has wide acceptance in competition with the product of every other country in the world.
It will be interesting to all hon. members, I am sure, to hear the figures I am about to give. In 1936 Denmark exported to the United Kingdom 100 million dozen eggs, while Canada exported one million dozen eggs. In other words, for every one hundred Danish eggs sold in the United Kingdom one Canadian egg was sold. And Danish eggs were sold at a premium of ten per cent. In 1936 Denmark exported 2,172,000 hundredweight of butter to the United Kingdom, while Canada exported 40,000 hundredweight; and the premium on Danish butter, even above New Zealand butter, was no less than twenty per cent. In 1936 Denmark exported to the United Kingdom 3,373,000 hundredweight of bacon, while Canada exported 1,092,000; that is, we were outsold three to one. And the Danish price was twelve per cent higher than ours.
Let us also realize the handicap under which Denmark has been operating. Our eggs have free entry into the market of the United Kingdom, whereas the duty against Denmark on this commodity is one shilling per great hundred. Canadian butter enters the British market duty free; the rate of duty against Danish butter is fifteen shillings per hundredweight. As regards bacon, it will be recalled that in the agreement with Denmark the United Kingdom among other things undertook not to regulate imports of bacon and ham unless necessary for the regulation of the marketing of domestic supplies, in which case the Danish allocation was not to be less than 62 per cent of the total permitted imports from foreign countries. With the permission of the committee I should like to have this table placed on Hansard in tabular form, giving as it does exports from Canada and exports from Denmark of bacon, butter and eggs from 1928 to 1937.

A further point that should be borne in mind is the extraordinary development of Danish cooperatives, a factor that has been of the utmost importance in the rise of Denmark to her present position. To complete the story within the limits of the moment is difficult; but let it be sufficient to say that it was in 1882 that the first cooperative was set up, while to-day there are 1,400 of them patronized by 192,000 out of the 204,000 fanners. The cooperatives to-day handle 90 per cent of the milk supply, 85 per cent of the bacon, 50 per cent of the butter, and 65 per cent of the feed and grains. Through the cooperatives the Danish farmer is assured of his market and the transportation of his products to it. He has no worries in regard to rates of foreign exchange or the problem

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
of the middleman or shipping. If he is efficient, he gets the top price. If he is not efficient, he has only himself to blame; for every possible aid is given him directly and on the ground by the educational branch of the cooperative societies, which societies are well backed up by and receive energetic support from the government. The result has been essentially the standardization of Danish agricultural production. A small farm set-up of ten acres will have four cows, two horses and three pigs. A medium sized farm, of seventy acres, will boast twenty-five cows, six horses, and twenty-eight pigs, and will also employ four labourers and one maid. So scientific is the farming in Denmark that virtually the cow may be regarded as a machine and the pig as raw material.
I have already stated that the whole basis upon which Danish agriculture is predicated is quality. Let us see for a moment what is done in regard to the three products we have discussed. Every solitary, single one of the 1,200,000,000 eggs which left Denmark last year for the United Kingdom was lamp-tested by government inspectors. Every barrel of butter that leaves the country is also passed by government inspectors; every pound of bacon the same. And not only are the pigs examined on the hoof by veterinary surgeons, but every part of that pig is also examined by a veterinary surgeon in the course of its passage through the slaughtery. Thus, if at any time an egg or a barrel of butter or a side of bacon fails to come up to the rigid standard set by the government, and is turned down by the inspector, that egg, that barrel of butter or that side of bacon does not leave the country.
From the farmer's point of view the cooperative is a tremendous boon. Take the story of cooperative butter making. The farmer, or probably his wife, milks night and morning of course, and puts the milk in cans at the farm gate in the morning. The truck from the local cooperative picks up the cans shortly afterwards and takes them to the creamery where the milk is made into butter under the most rigid inspection. Next morning, when the cooperative truck again stops at his farm, it leaves the cans of the day before, this time full of the skim milk, picks up the whole milk cans and carries them to the creamery. That is all the farmer has to do with the processing and marketing of his butter, but he rceives back the skim milk which he feeds to his pigs.
A similar story can be told in regard to bacon. As a quota is placed on the market so is the production controlled; the farmer each year receives so many " pig cards,"
which permit him to export as bacon to the United Kingdom the number of pigs for which he receives cards, nine, fifteen, twenty-five or whatever it may be, depending on the size of his farm. His pigs are bred only from government registered stock. Let me say in passing that every head of live stock and even every chicken in Denmark is registered. Unless the farmer can prove beyond doubt that not only the parents but also the four grandparents as well of his animals are approved by the government, the farmer cannot breed from that stock. It is only from government approved stock that breeding is permitted. Thus the strain of Danish cattle, horses, pigs, sheep and chickens is maintained to an amazingly high degree of perfection and efficiency.
To come back to the pigs, the farmer feeds his pigs in accordance with the best recognized methods. When they reach the weight of 170 pounds he rings up the cooperative slaughtery, which calls for them and takes them to town. On the hoof they are examined by a veterinary surgeon; if they weigh between 168 and 172 pounds and pass the inspector, they are slaughtered. If the pig weighs less than 168 pounds, it is returned to the farmer for further feeding; if it weighs over 172 pounds, it is also returned to the farmer; but in this case he cannot attempt to reduce its weight, he will fatten it and send it to Germany, where a fatter bacon is desired.
Hon. members will recognize from what I have said as briefly as possible that the Danish government has taken extraordinarily effective steps, working in conjunction with the cooperatives, to develop a great product which is acceptable in the market to which it is sent.
All that I have said thus far is in no way intended as criticism of the efforts of the Canadian farmer.

I appreciate your courtesy, Mr. Chairman, and that of the committee. As I have said, and I repeat, the Canadian farmer is himself without a peer in the world. But it seems to me that the government of this dominion can take many steps which have yet to be taken to assist the

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
farmer in the development of his products, so that they may be acceptable on a basis of quality and kind to the consumers of the market to which they are sent. What I have endeavoured to point out is that the Canadian farmer possesses potentialities which have not been fully developed. Our farmers have done their best and done it well; what remains to be done it seems to me is the direct responsibility of the government. The example of Denmark is before us when it was realized that the Danish farmer on his farm could not possibly know the quality and kind of product required for successful marketing in the British market. His government ascertained that, conveyed the information to him, and gave him every possible assistance in attaining that standard.
The minister, in speaking last evening, as reported on page 2992 of Hansard, said:
The Danish people have a line of hogs which have been bred up to standard during the last two hundred years.
Perhaps the minister will permit me to disagree with that statement. The Danish hog of fifty years ago was completely dissimilar to the Danish hog of to-day.
Is that not the way you get a different type, by breeding up to it?

Yes; I was referring only
to the length of time taken.
I have the official report which indicates it has been 200 years

Let me describe the Danish hog of 1880 and now. The 1938 model of Danish bacon hog is long and deep of body, with flat back, lean, and short of leg, whereas the Danish hog of the 1880's was thick, short, big of body, arched of back, and long of leg. The 1938 model is essentially a streamlined model. Bacon from the 1880 model would not find a place on the English breakfast table of to-day. Accordingly the hog that one now sees in Denmark was developed so that its bacon would find that place which it has found.
Eggs, butter and bacon are the only products which I have discussed this afternoon. In the case of eggs and butter our surplus is comparatively small; therefore we export comparatively little. But is it not a government responsibility to take the steps necessary to create an increasing demand for Canadian eggs, butter and bacon in the United Kingdom, and thus open up to the Canadian farmer the possibility of marketing these products on a larger scale? There is no reason why we should produce only so many eggs, or only the amount of butter or bacon that

we do produce, except the restriction of the market available. The farmer himself cannot develop the market, but the government can. I am not for a moment losing sight of the fact that our domestic market has been, is and always should be our most important market; but there is no reason why Canada cannot take full advantage of the possibilities of an export market as safe and secure as that of the United Kingdom, made possible to us under the agreements of 1932, reaffirmed in 1937.
Any thinking Canadian who considers the trends cannot but be alarmed at the rise of urbanization in this dominion. During the last eight or nine years there has been a sharp increase in our urban population at the expense of the rural population. That obviously means one thing, that those who would normally remain on the farms are forsaking them and coming into the cities to seek their fortune there. Hon. members know too well that there is great difficulty to-day in keeping the farmers' sons on the farm. Why? Not because farming is unattractive; not because the difficulties of farming are too much for our younger generation-far from it-but because farming in so many cases has proved unprofitable. Therefore, what might be a gainful and worthy occupation appears as wasted drudgery to the young people. What makes it unprofitable? The fact that the prices of produce are out of line, for one thing, and loss of markets for another. These two combine to promote hard times for the farmer.
The unemployment situation in our urban centres continues to be one of our greatest national problems. For that problem there is only one solution; that is jobs. If farming can be restored to the position of a profitable and gainful occupation, it will go an immeasurably long way towards solving our unemployment problem. Again let me quote Denmark. There the government has acquired large tracts of land, which it breaks up into ten and fifteen acre farms. The would-be young farmer merely has to show that he has $200 or more in his possession and the necessary qualifications to be a farmer. He is then given a ten or fifteen acre farm, completely equipped with barn, house and live stock. He does not have to pay back a single penny except as he earns. I am not suggesting that such a course could be followed here; but I am sure hon. members will agree that some steps can be taken in the development of our markets, in the stabilization of the prices of farm products, which will make farming attractive, and this will not only tend

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
to retain our farming youth upon the farms, but will also further attract many of the farming youth, who have come to our cities, back to the farm, thus relieving the acute unemployment situation existing in our cities to-day.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, permit me to state that I am not unmindful of the burden of the recommendations of the Shaw report, or the proposals already claimed to be made effective by the minister, as reported on page 10 of his recently released bulletin; but I find, looking through the recommendations and proposals of the Shaw report, a great lack of two factors which, it seems to me, are the most singularly important part of any governmental effort directly to assist the Canadian farmer. That is, namely: (1) a program designed to raise the standard of Canadian live stock and thus, Canadian products, by direct assistance to the farmer-a program designed to make sure, beyond peradventure, that the efforts of the farmers are directed in the most profitable channels to produce butter, eggs, bacon, cheese and other such products adequately suited to the market to which they are to be exported, and (2) a program to stabilize farm product prices.
In regard to the first factor I earnestly urge upon the minister, with all the earnestness of which I am capable, that he give immediate thought to a governmental program of direct educational assistance to the Canadian farmer that will permit him to take advantage of the markets which are open to him, particularly the market of the United Kingdom. We must, perforce, realize that important and all as it Still is in the development of Canada, we cannot depend upon wheat alone as the outstanding product of our farms. Through no fault of our own we have lost many of our best customers for this commodity. Thus, further steps must be taken forthwith to take up the slack in agriculture, and it would seem to me to be of the utmost importance to the dominion as a whole that this entire matter be given the full and concentrated attention, not only of the government of the day, but of the governments that are to follow; for prosperous farms in Canada mean a prosperous Canada.
The Canadian farm and the Canadian farmer form, together, a part of Canada of an importance that cannot be overestimated. Justly we are proud of the progress we have made through the years; but in the discussion which the committee has permitted me this afternoon I have tried to throw out to the government of the day a suggestion or two which, if applied in practice, will result
in the even higher development of the Canadian farm, and which will help relieve the difficulties which our farmers have been forced to face.
In regard to the second factor, no mention is made in the report of what may be regarded as the greatest problem faced by agriculture to-day, namely stabilized prices. There could be no more efficacious boon to the Canadian farmer than efficient steps taken toward the stabilization of prices of farm products.
What steps?

As I have already stated in this chamber, I do not pose as an economist, but I fully realize that the law of supply and demand as it at present operates in this country is operating to the severe detriment of the Canadian farmer. Other factors as well, which need not 'be discussed here, have tended toward extraordinary low levels in the prices of our farm products. Surely, it must be by this time obvious to the government of the day that some artificial means, through legislation or otherwise, will have to be employed to stabilize prices. And, Mr. Chairman, we must all recognize that the lot of the farmer in Canada will never be very much better than it is to-day until these steps are taken.
In speaking in this chamber, not so long ago, the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) used language as reported at page 101 of Hansard to which I direct the attention of hon. members. To this I shall add nothing further, but merely say, as I take my seat, that I urge upon the government that a program designed to aid the fanner directly by assisting him in the development of his product to fit the market in which he sells be stimulated at once, and that some plan be formulated and put into effect to stabilize farm product prices. To this there can be only one result-a more stable and more secure Canada, and a greater and more united Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) speaking on the question of marketing, painted a rather gloomy picture of the activities of the cheese producers' association. I should like to make a few remarks with regard to this question.
For many years the dairymen had two organizations in Ontario, the eastern and the western Ontario dairymen's association. I believe they served a useful purpose for a considerable length of time. But the farmers of the eastern district formed the impression that those associations had survived their period of usefulness, and the feeling sprang up among
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

the dairymen that they needed a newer and more active organization to further their interests. Because of that the cheese producers' association came into being.
The first encouragement received was from the Hon. Mr. Weir, the minister of agriculture for the dominion at that time. The first financial assistance was received from the provincial department of agriculture operating under the Hon. Thomas Kennedy.
Their first objective was to have all cheese boarded, thereby cutting out factories selling on board rulings with the idea of stimulating a healthy competition among the buyers. Secondly, they wished to ascertain by trial shipments to Great Britain if there was too great a spread between the price paid to the producer in Canada and the price paid by the consumer in Great Britain. They made a small profit on this experiment in 1936, and sustained a loss in 1937. While there was a small loss suffered in 1937 the thought lingers in the minds of the producing farmers that the cheese exporters narrowed their margin of profit when the cheese producers made their trial shipments to the old land, with a view to driving the producers' association out of the picture, and although it appears as a small loss it may be an actual gain in dollars and cents to the farmers of Ontario.
The Ontario Marketing Act gave them the power to collect five cents on each hundred pounds of cheese manufactured, which works out at about half a cent per hundred pounds of milk. The national dairy council have been depending on voluntary contributions and the response has not been as generous as they would like. By this method of financing the association everybody makes a fair contribution to the expenses of the association and more general satisfaction is promoted among the farmers.
I have made these observations in order to convey to the committee the actual situation in regard to cheese associations.

What does the hon.
member for Greenwood say would become of Denmark if we were to secure the market they have at the present time?

I do not consider for a
moment that the market of the United Kingdom has been exhausted. There is room for both Denmark and Canada.

It seems to me the discussion which might have taken place under this item was pretty well exhausted under another item discussed some time ago. Hon. members may think there has been undue discussion, but since this is an entirely new

set-up within the department I think it is fair to say we were entitled to the information for which we have been asking.
It is my intention at this time to direct only one or two questions to the minister, and then I shall have finished with at least this part of the discussion. There are some points in regard to the set-up which are not yet clear in my mind. For instance, at the heads of the different branches of the department we have gentlemen who have served in their capacities for some time. Are those gentlemen now acting in a dual capacity; that is, are they serving, for instance, under the marketing services branch and under the production services branch, or has their work been changed so that each serves under one branch?

These men are not
serving in two capacities; they serve in one capacity in administering the work of a certain branch of which they are in charge. For example, Doctor Hilton is still in charge of the health of animals branch, but his work is carried on under the director of production. That is just an illustration.

Does the dairy commissioner
act in a dual capacity, or does the head of the sheep and swine division?

Practically all of our
services having to do with dairy products relate to marketing. The greater part of the production is attended to by the provinces. We take care of the marketing end, and look after inspections which have to do with the grades of products, a service wrhich is considered to be part of the marketing operation. Naturally that work is carried on under the marketing branch.

I thank the minister for the
information he has given. I should like to make one more reference to the mark which has been discussed under another item. Clause (c) of the recommendation states that the right to use this mark, where it is not compulsory, will be granted only to producers under licence. I should like to know why the producers are put in a different class from exporters generally and commission men. It looks to me as though there is discrimination or a monopoly is being set up.

As I said earlier, the
details have not been worked out completely, but if there is to be licensing, it will apply right through. Anyone using the mark will have to be licensed to use it, whether he is a producer or a jobber.

Has any program
been devised for the stabilization of prices?

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
As one having a direct contact with farming operations, it is my opinion that if we could stabilize prices to any satisfactory degree, our production would far outstrip our ability to sell. In the area from which I come the productive power is tremendous in eggs, bacon, beef and everything that we have been discussing. Just about the time a farmer gets into pigs, as they say, just about the time that he equips himself so that he can produce, for some unaccountable reason prices come down and stay down until he is forced out of swine production. Then prices go up again when the farmer has no equipment with which to take advantage of the increase. There may be some inevitable and insuperable natural law which brings this about, but I seriously doubt it. If we could tackle the problem at that point it seems to me we would be well on the way to a solution of our difficulty.
Then there is another obstacle facing the farmer. Frequently when prices rise to a point at which farmers can "make a go," as they say, when they reach a point at which they can make things pay, then the prices of feeds and other ingredients that go into their production begin to rise. I have heard many good farmers say that by no means whatsoever can you figure your way out to a profit. So long as such conditions exist our productive power will simply be lying dormant.

There has been no concerted effort, other than that which was put forth under the Natural Products Marketing Act, to stabilize prices. As the hon. member knows, that act was declared ultra vires, but certain activities have been carried on by the provinces since it was declared ultra vires. However, there has been an attempt made in other directions indirectly to stabilize prices upward. Attempts have been made to improve the grades and increase the consumption of certain of our farm products, and the result has been an improvement in prices. I think I am correct when I say that the increase in the annual per capita consumption of butter in Canada was 4-06 pounds from 1925 to 1936. The fact that our butter was improved in quality had something to do with the greater consumption in Canada. The fact that we have had a greater consumption has had something to do with prices having been better in recent years.
I do not know that I can say much more in regard to the point raised. It is always a question whether you can set a price for a product and maintain it. I presume that if a country is sufficiently small and the product is sufficiently standardized you might be able
to do it, provided all of the output is consumed within the country. But even a country as small as Denmark, which markets its product in Great Britain, is not able to say what price is going to be paid in Great Britain. Their prices go up and down just as ours do. Britain has much more regulation through cooperative organizations than we have, yet they have not been able to stabilize prices. The most they have been able to do is to stabilize their commodities and create a demand in a market that is more or less constant.
Some of us listened to an address to-day by an extremely well informed man from Great Britain, Sir Reginald Dorman Smith. He took a different position regarding some matters referred to in the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) in connection with the relationship between Great Britain and Denmark and other countries. I am not prepared at the moment to say which point of view is the correct one. However, the remarks made on that occasion would indicate that this stabilization is more nearly possible in a country that consumes all its own agricultural products than it is in one that consumes only seventy per cent of its production and sells the other thirty per cent outside the country. It is probably even more difficult to do it in a country where you consume only thirty per cent and ship out seventy per cent of your production, as we do with one of our products. These are some of the difficulties with which we are confronted. I do not think there is any one standard that can be set in a country with an area so widespread as ours in connection with price control or the standardization of products. However, we are attempting to accomplish results by applying suitable remedies to the varying conditions that exist in this country.

I wish to direct the attention of the minister to a demonstration of price stabilization of farm products which has taken place in New Zealand. New Zealand produces large quantities of cheese and butter and exports the bulk of this production. Yet she has successfully stabilized the prices of both butter and cheese. She is able to guarantee a price of twenty-five cents for butter and something like fifteen cents per pound for cheese, using the current rates of exchange between New Zealand and the motherland. New Zealand, with a small population but producing vast quantities of these commodities, has demonstrated very successfully that a certain amount of stabilization can be undertaken under conditions

Supply-Agriculture-M arketing
dissimilar to those outlined by the minister. This is not the time to enter into any academic discussion or we shall never reach the end of these estimates, -but I wanted to draw that to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture.

It is not any too clear to me just where the dividing line is between the marketing activities of the Department of Agriculture and the marketing activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but it is quite obvious that the intention of the minister is to improve the opportunities of marketing our products. I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the difficulty we have had in the past of informing the buying public of what we have to sell and where it can be bought. I shall deal with one side of this question as it applies to this country. For many years past we have tried to sell British Columbia fruit in the prairie provinces, and I know of no more annoying type of letter to receive than the one which contains the statement, " Your fruit is fine but we do not know where to get it." When we take that difficulty back to those who are responsible for distributing the fruit or vegetables, as we always do, we are informed that apparently that whole prairie country has been divided up into territories and adequately served, and in some cases I must say that when the matter is run down to the bottom we find that the consumer did not use any too much gumption in endeavouring to obtain that produce. But still the difficulty is there. Where the produce is available it seems to be very difficult to get it into the head of the consumer that there it can be bought, and any assistance the minister is able to give through his officers in informing the buying public of the produce there is to sell, so much the better for the producer.
I want for a moment to refer to the other side of it, and that is the difficulty which occurs in Great Britain, in informing the British public of the produce Canada has to sell. I notice in the April number of Overseas an article headed, Empire Table Exchange. It is a description of what had recently been seen by the writer at the British Industries Fair, and I want to quote a couple of paragraphs:
Decidedly, Canadian bacon was the best on show. (The whole Canadian exhibit was first class.) I asked where it could be procured in London, and was told " at any big shop." I tried at a shop which is among our biggest, and has a transatlantic name. It was selling only Wiltshire and Danish. Danish bacon is excellent, but I asked why the money shouldn't be kept in the family. I was then asked, seriously and with a wish to know, whether Canadian

bacon was good, etc. In the long run I received a promise that it should be available in a week. But why did the B.I.F. Canadian officials think it could be bought when it couldn't?
This leads directly to a consideration which I hope overseas readers will pardon to an ardent friend of their produce, who wants to see Empire Table Exchange becoming more intense and more fruitful every week. I do not know what overseas housewives are like as regards new comestibles, but at home in England they are absurdly unadventurous, largely because the Englishman is very conservative in his food. They see a new thing (as once they must have seen the first tomato, as some time before Nell Gwynn they must have seen a fruit that they didn't then know was an orange), and they say: "What's that?" and the greengrocer says: "I don't know, mum; I bought a couple on chance." She doesn't buy any, and he purchases no more.
The relatively small expense of sending quantities of leaflets with empire exports to England (and to inter-empire markets) should be no hindrance to an activity of which the importance cannot be exaggerated. It is not enough to say that this tuber can be treated in various ways; a half dozen amusing, interesting recipes (and printed on good paper, in clear type, and clearly set out) will help the retail seller and the ordinary customer to increase the market. We all want to vary our menu, we all want to buy empire; but you have to help us. I think that even Canadian apples, which are so attractive to look at. ought to wear a badge of "for dessert," "for baking."
As I said when I commenced, I do not know because I do not understand the dividing line between the minister's department and Trade and Commerce in this matter, but the object of his marketing branch is undoubtedly to foster marketing, and if the minister would take into consideration the desirability and the possibility of increasing the information which reaches the prospective empire buyer in Great Britain he will have accomplished a great deal.

Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that I can be justly accused of having taken too much of the time of the house since my arrival here, but I should like to make a few remarks upon this particular item, affording as it does the opportunity to give expression to views which I have held now for some few years with regard to agriculture, and in particular dairying, coming as I do from a dairying section of the country.
Agriculture, as we all know, is the oldest of human occupations, and it would appear to me that it should be the most paying of all human activities. But unfortunately it is not. The whole nation, and I might say the whole world, should be keenly aware of the importance to all the people of a prosperous agriculture. But unfortunately this conviction

Supply-Agriculture-M arketing
does not seem to prevail amongst all, because it has been stated, and quite truly, I believe, by Sir Josiah Stamp, that:
The world as a whole, over a given length of time, has almost certainly been fed below cost for the last hundred years.
The farm problem can be stated in four words: Farm profits are inadequate. The disparity between the income of farm enterprise and the returns from the investment of equal labour, capital and managerial ability in industrial effort, is apparent to all those who have examined the facts; and neither the welfare of the people directly nor the national good itself can decently suffer the agricultural population to continue under the definite handicap of producing below cost.
I understand that the farm problem is not simply one but many. There are some forms of assistance that take effect quickly, and others only in the course of time. Amongst the aids in the former category I might mention transportation as being vital to agriculture. In the United States six per cent of the gross annual production is said to be absorbed by freight rates. Commercial attaches should find and develop a market as "international trade is primarily dependent upon international understanding and amity." More can be done to educate foreign peoples to a taste for the foods from Canadian farms. Probably the most important of all steps towards creating a permanent and growing demand for Canadian food-stuffs on the menus of the world is 1he maintenance of world peace and the diffusion of friendly understanding. Other means are agricultural colleges, research work and extension services.
Agriculture needs the greatest consideration from all governments, and especially is this true with respect to dairying, which represents nineteen per cent of the total agricultural revenue, whereas wheat represented in 1930 only fourteen per cent of the total agricultural wealth of the country. The dairy farmer has been losing money for a number of years, and the loss has been heavy enough for the farmer who can ship to the fluid milk market, but more has been lost by the dairy farmers who have been shipping to local cheese and butter factories. In support of my statement that the dairy farmer has been losing money, I should like to cite data obtained on two surveys in the province of Quebec in 1931-32, which are reported on in the report of the minister of agriculture for the province for that year.
The first data, which I shall present in a very cursory way, relates to the fluid milk
market, and the second data to the dairy farmers who have been shipping their products to local cheese and butter factories.
In 1931-32 an economic investigation was carried on in the Montreal district and in the counties around the city of Montreal. The number of farms investigated was 182, and the number of animal units 4,106. The report of this investigation was to the effect that in 1934 fluid milk sold at Montreal for $1.44 per hundred pounds, whereas the cost of production was SI .97 per hundred pounds. A similar investigation was carried on in the county of Megantic, comprising fifty farms in that county; its object was to determine the cost of the production of milk by farmers selling to butter or cheese factories, and the gist of this report was that it cost the farmers $1.44 to produce one hundred pounds of milk, and at that time the gross selling price of that one hundred pounds of milk was 72 cents, a net of sixty cents, showing thereby a loss of 84 cents per hundred pounds by each dairy producer. I believe these figures show that the assertion that the dairy producer is producing at a loss is well founded. I trust that it will be the endeavour of the Department of Agriculture to do all that they can to enhance the revenue of the farmers and especially the dairy farmers of the country.

The minister said something about retests in the areas that have been under accreditation for some time and are restricted areas. In the light of past experience, how nearly is this test satisfactory and how nearly have the restricted areas been kept clean of tuberculosis?
I think the best answer to that is to call attention to what has happened in some districts where the work has been carried on.
Yes.

This list shows the restricted areas for the eradication of bovine tuberculosis in which infection has been reduced to one half of one per cent and less. In Prince Edward Island the entire province, comprised of the counties of Kings, Queens and Prince, has been reduced to one half of one per cent. In New Brunswick nine counties have been similarly reduced; in Quebec 16; in Ontario 6; in Manitoba 1; in Saskatchewan 13; in British Columbia 1.

That seems to be a very satisfactory situation. Can the minister give us any information as to what happens in the case of accredited herds that are not in restricted areas? Has the experience been similar in that respect?
The results in those are almost identical.
Would the minister give us the names of the six areas in Ontario which have been accepted but not yet tested?
Province of Ontario: Peterborough county, Lanark county, Island of St. Joseph, Simcoe, Victoria and the Rainy River district.
Waterloo is not included?
No.
Or Haldimand?
It is not in that group.
We have heard considerable this afternoon about streamlining of the pig. I wondered if that has affected the genera! health of the animal.
I am informed that it does not affect the health.

Judging from the information given by the minister we are quite a way behind meeting the demands of the cattle breeders in this country. Many of them think that a more determined effort should be made to eradicate tuberculosis. I have been in close touch with the cattle breeders of Ontario this winter, as well as with those in the western provinces, and I know that they are exercised about the inability, shall I say, of the department to keep up with their demands. For that reason I support the suggestion of the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) who believes that we should have a larger appropriation for this work. I am not going to enlarge upon that phase of the subject to-day, but there is one observation which I wish to make in this connection. Yesterday the minister, in answer to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) I believe, said that the experimental stage in connection with Bang's disease was about the same as it was in connection with tuberculosis some years ago. That, I believe, is true. For that reason we cannot undertake a wholesale policy to eliminate Bang's disease, but I suggest that we might follow a policy such as we adopted in regard to tuberculosis and start with accredited herds. After all, that is the nursery of the whole industry in Canada, and in my opinion we should begin with those herds in attempting to eliminate Bang's disease. We have been successful in eradicating tuberculosis because we had the cooperation of the breeders as well as of the government departments, and it seems to me that we must also have the cooperation of the breeders if we are to eliminate Bang's disease. I do not believe that we. will get that cooperation.
Is it not a fact that the treatment of Bang's disease is still in the experimental stage?

Yes, I agree with that; and for that very reason I do not think that we shall get the cooperation of the breeders. Farmers who have valuable live stock will not have their cattle condemned for Bang's disease unless they receive some compensation, and that is why I suggest that we should start with the accredited herds and pay compensation to breeders, who will get at least something for any loss they may sustain if their cattle are slaughtered. I suggest that the minister seriously consider the advisability of compensating farmers for the loss of cattle on account of Bang's disease, and that he should start with the accredited herds of the country.

Has the regulation been changed to give compensation for grade cattle?

Supply-Agriculture-M arketing

Yes. In the accredited areas they get compensation for grade cattle as well as the others. I have here a list of tests made for tuberculosis beginning in 1915-16. In that year there were 2,937 and this last year the number was 1,349,468. The development has been gradual from 2,937 in 1915-16 up to close to a million and a half last year, and I think that illustrates in another way the position we are in in relation to Bang's disease. The authorities in the first instance had to convince the breeders that the test was a reliable one. I find that in every delegation of breeders who come to my office to discuss the matter there is a difference of opinion among them as to whether the test is reliable or not. As regards tuberculosis they readily admit that twenty-five years ago they did not believe that the test was reliable. The first task of the department is therefore to establish confidence in the minds of the breeders that the test is reliable and when that is done, the next step might be given consideration. Eor the time being, however, the department is trying to establish that confidence in the minds of breeders.
Is there a reliable treatment?
The department thinks so, but we have not been able to convince everyone else. We have not been able to convince the majority of those interested in herds that it is.

The statement the minister made a little while ago would indicate that Saskatchewan is pretty healthy so far as cattle are concerned. Do I understand that in the retesting there was less than one and a half per cent?
It was one-half of one per cent.
That makes it better. What was paid in Saskatchewan by way of compensation in the last year, and what is the average?
I have not that information here, but I could get it compiled.

The minister says that the department is attempting to establish confidence not only in the test for Bang's, but also in the treatment. I understand that the treatment is a serum which is injected. Is the federal department taking any steps to supply that serum when it is applied for, or is that left entirely to the provincial authorities?

So far as the test is concerned, the remark I made a few moments ago in reply to a question by the hon. member
for Swift Current was that the department was fairly confident that the test was reliable. So far as the treatment is concerned, the serum provided for injection into calves, that is purely in the experimental stage, and we are not in a position to make any pronouncements. It is merely a matter of checking the serum at the present time.
Is the department taking any steps to provide the serum or is that left entirely to the provinces?
The department is not supplying it to the provinces but only to institutions under the control of the department itself, so that we may experiment with it.
But I understand that a serum is being used extensively in the country. Where is it obtained? I believe it is being used with very beneficial effects.
Bringing it in is prohibited by law. I am not in a position to say whether someone is bootlegging it into the country and using it. It is illegal to use it.

There is a serious situation in Saskatchewan, brought about to a considerable extent by the policy adopted last fall of shipping cattle out of the drought areas. The policy which was adopted by the provincial government and endorsed and carried out by the federal Department of Agriculture dealt a very serious blow to the live

stock and dairying industry in that province, a blow from which I do not think they can recover in the next ten years. Early last fall when this policy was adopted many protests were made by individual farmers, rural municipalities and boards of trade. I had many protests come to me asking me to make representations to have the department change their policy. The minister will remember that early in September I wrote him asking that he give consideration to the dairymen, especially the small men with eight or ten or twelve cows in the eastern part of Saskatchewan. He was good enough to reply stating that the matter was more or less up to the provincial government. I had also taken it up with them, and their reply was that they had to enforce their rules strictly, cutting down the stock to not more than four cows on a farm in that district.
I hope I did not say it was up to the provincial government.

The minister referred me
to the minister of agriculture for Saskatchewan. Mr. Taggart replied to the effect that he did not think it would be possible to supply sufficient feed.

That is different from
what the hon. member was saying. I understood him to say that I said it was up v,o the provincial department.
The minister's letter referred me to the department of agriculture in Saskatchewan.

To put the record right, the hon. member is making a speech which might be presumed to apply to one thing when it probably applies to another. As far as the movement of live stock out of the drought area is concerned, the federal government is absolutely responsible for that policy; the Saskatchewan government had nothing to do with it.

I have here form 626B37
issued by the provincial government-

Moving the cattle out
of the drought area was a policy decided upon by the federal government entirely. We asked the province to assist us in carrying it into effect; but no responsibility for the policy rests on the province; it rests entirely on this government.

Well, that makes it all
the worse. I suppose the minister would say it would be impossible to get feed to maintain any more than the number allowed to be kept; that is, four on a farm. I made

certain investigations with respect to feed that could be procured, in Manitoba particularly ; individuals and representatives of rural municipalities had gone down there and were putting up feed, and I also drove through part of the country myself. This is a serious matter, and I take this opportunity of expressing my disapproval of the policy carried out last fall in this respect. We know the importance of dairying; we know what it means to the farmer who has been milking eight or ten cows, and who must meet grocery bills and other expenses. It has meant considerable to him to have had a reduction in stock.

We have spent the

We are on the item

Does the hon. member object at this time to the removal of cattle out of Saskatchewan last fall to the feeding grounds in other provinces?
