I believe the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is now discussing a matter pertaining to agricultural distress, a subject which has been before the house for a considerable length of time this session, and [DOT] one the discussion of which lasted a great many days. I have listened carefully to the hon. gentleman's observations, and I
must ask him to confine his remarks to the item under discussion, namely live stock and poultry, production services.
If the Chairman rules that the production of dairy cattle does not come under this item, then I certainly am out of order.

It seems to me there is a good deal in what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has said with respect to the supply of bulls for the production of cattle. He raised the point, as reported in Hansard at page 2540, and received the following reply from the minister:
I regret very much to have to advise that it is not possible to encourage the farmers in the Alexander district to organize an association to apply for the loan of a pure bred bull from this department this year. We have already received from Saskatchewan applications greatly in excess of the number of suitable bulls which it will be possible to purchase, and have been under the necessity of refusing consideration to nearly two hundred inquiries received from Saskatchewan alone.
This reply would indicate that the government has reached the point of frustration, and something determined should be done to remedy such a situation. Has the minister's department investigated the possibilities of artificial insemination. Science has indicated that artificial insemination is entirely practical, and I am informed that successful practice is not attended by any very technical difficulties. If this matter were studied, and some move made in connection with it, we might solve some of the present difficulties in the situation. We might not have to wait a matter of ten years before increasing the number of cattle to a normal point.

I understand Russia claims to be producing successfully through the process of artificial insemination. Our department is keeping in close touch with activities in that direction, but at present we are not in a position to deal with a situation such as that existing in the west.
With regard to that portion of the remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle which have to do with the bull policy, I would say that under the policy we are putting more bulls into Saskatchewan than we are putting into any other part of Canada. The reason is the one which has been outlined, namely that great difficulty has been experienced in the feeding of live stock in that province in the last few years. There is probably another reason why we should be very careful. Probably in days past we have made some mistakes in certain parts of
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

Saskatchewan. Only a few years ago one could walk into a bank in Saskatchewan and see on the walls an invitation to borrow money to secure bulls. That may have had something to do with our having so much live stock in certain sections that it was necessary to move it out. More careful investigations will have to be made when we begin to reestablish the herds in those areas, and we shall have to decide whether or not it is good policy under existing conditions to reestablish them in certain sections. In order to meet the situation which exists in the area in which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is interested, an area in which it has been pretty well established that stock rasing in a substantial way is a proper part of the agriculture of that district, something should be done to reestablish the herds. But there are certain sections to which we shall have to give very close investigation before proceeding.
I believe in the past year there has been a change in the policy of the department in connection with stallions in Saskatchewan.
Yes.

Complaints I have had were that the notifications regarding clubbing were received by owners too late in the season. Would that come under the federal department-, or was that decision promulgated by the provincial department of agriculture?

The premium was paid on a fifty-fifty basis. The province pays $2.50 and we pay the same amount. However, the clubbing policy is under federal jurisdiction, and is still being carried on. The premium policy has been discontinued in Saskatchewan, our main reason being that we were carrying on both activities in that province and were not doing so in the other western provinces. We are now confining our activities to the one branch in Saskatchewan, as is being done in the other provinces.
When was that notification made?

I .think it was some time in February. There was some difficulty in some of the areas in forming clubs after the notification went out. I know, however, that quite a number did form clubs after that time.

There was considerable difficulty in some areas. I am thinking of an area in my own constituency where on account of weather and other conditions the owners did not receive notification until a time too late in the season to form clubs.

The result is that these horses are in the barns. The .owners have been suffering from drought, and they really cannot afford to maintain the animals and give the service they have been giving for the past several years.

There must be some duplication in connection with the vote for live stock and poultry. I notice that under item No. 11, which deals with live stock and poultry under the heading "marketing services," there is an increase of $54,928. Then we come down to item No. 16, and we find that it deals with live stock and .poultry, under the heading "production services," and shows an increase of $95,112.50. The minister has been good enough to give the details concerning the 895,112.50, but I have not heard anything about the other amount. I do not wish him to repeat what has been said-probably I should have been in the house-but I should like to know why on the same page there should be two items with respect to live stock and poultry, one for about half a million and the other for almost a full million, one with an increase of more than $54,000 and the other with one of more than $95,000. The minister goes on to tell us that there has been an increase in the cost of automobiles as well as for prizes, bonuses and premiums. There is an increase of $11,000 for buildings and lands, but that is not much in this committee. Then there is an increase of $20,000 in travelling expenses. Is the business increasing so rapidly that travelling expenses must increase to such an extent? What are we getting out of all this? If any one is receiving a benefit, I have no objection, but I am afraid a lot of it is being wasted. The minister has not the time to go into all these matters in detail, and I think an investigation should be held into them. I do not accuse any one of doing anything wrong, but if this sort of thing is going on there is not much use in hon. members protesting against it all the time when no attention is paid to their protests.

This goes back to the question that was raised a few moments ago, I think by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn), as to the division between marketing and production. I think the discussion we have just had with regard to bulls and stallions is a clear indication of the difference in the two policies. For many years the federal Department of Agriculture has been taking an interest in the improvement of live stock in Canada, which is purely a production activity. We have just passed a vote having to do with the health of animals, which work is carried on for the purpose of improving

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
production. We are now dealing with a section of the vote which concerns the breeding of live stock and the production of better bulls, better stallions and better sires generally. Any activity in connection with the marketing of this stock comes under the marketing branch. I do not think there should be any difficulty about understanding this. There may be some opposition to the amount we are spending, but I cannot see why there should be any difficulty in understanding the difference between marketing and production.
Are results being obtained from the marketing branch?

Our friends who have been speaking seem to think we are not doing enough. Whenever we have tried to cut down in this work, objections have been raised. When we attempted to cut down in the work in Quebec in connection with the supplying of bulls, strong objection was made. I think it will be found generally across Canada that these services are quite necessary. The demand from one end of Canada to the other is for an extension rather than a discontinuance of the services.

I am quite in agreement with what the minister has said. I think these services are quite necessary. If I were to offer any criticism of the department, it would be that not enough money is being expended on this work. The minister stated that the premium policy in Saskatchewan has been discontinued in connection with rams and boars.

The premium policy applies all through eastern Canada, and there has been no change in that. In the western provinces we have had a club policy which suited their conditions better than the premium policy. About four or five years ago there was some activity started in Saskatchewan in connection with a premium policy, and this year we took the position that either one of two things must be done-we must have both policies all the way across Canada, or we must continue either the one or the other in the province. We decided to discontinue the premium policy in Saskatchewan.
What results are being obtained from the experiments which are being conducted in connection with landrace hogs? Perhaps this question might better be asked under the experimental farms vote.

I think it would be
better to leave it.

Would the minister give
us the latest figures with respect to the number of horses and dairy cows in Saskatchewan?

An order for a return
was asked for, I believe by the hon. member, which would contain those figures. I have not them available at the moment.

I regret that we cannot
get the information we ask for with respect to items of this kind.

I am quite sure that if the information has been asked for, it will be obtained eventually. The estimates referred to in the order were not these. There will be plenty of opportunities to discuss these matters when the supplementaries are brought down. There was also an opportunity earlier in the session when we were discussing the warrants.

What item is that in the
supplementaries ?
Provision will be made for all the matters that were discussed a few moments ago.

That item in the supplementaries passed at one sitting of the committee, and on the suggestion of the minister it was allowed to go through. Certain details were asked for which we could not get on that occasion, and the minister promised that on a later occasion they would be provided.

That will all come
up under the supplementaries covering similar work.

I notice there is a sharp
division of opinion among the members of the official opposition in connection with these expenditures I dare say that if a comparison were made of the expenditures on agriculture with those of other departments, serious discrepancies would be disclosed.

Supply-Agriculture-Plant Inspection

What care is being
taken at our ports of entry to prevent tourists and travellers bringing in fruit which might contain dangerous insects?

There are men located
at the important ports where the traffic is heavy to check fruit plants that might be subject to disease. At points where men are not located, the customs officials cooperate in checking everything that enters. If there is necessity to refer anything for further inspection, this is done.

Are we as stringent on
this side of the line as they are in the United States? I am thinking particularly of the state of Washington. I was referring to the small parcels of fruit that the tourist might have in his car. He may eat some of this and then throw the rest away.

There is practically the same condition prevailing in connection with fruit as there is in connection with animals. We have reciprocity with the federal government of the United States as far as regulations are concerned, but the regulations put out by the different states might not conform exactly with ours.

Would this item cover
the inspection of containers such as sacking and other things of that kind?

Wrappings and that
kind of thing are taken care of by the inspection under the health of animals vote. That inspection is carried on to prevent the entry of foot and mouth disease and diseases of that kind which might be carried in on the wrappings of plants.
That item passed, I understand.
Yes.
Would the minister permit me to make one very brief observation?
Certainly.

I am not complaining about the officials of the department doing their duty. I think it is very necessary and very desirable to guard against the entry of materials in the form of wrappers or packing for any class of goods that may contain disease from some other country. But a case came to my attention recently, and I could cite a number of them, where I think the department by cooperating with the importer could quite effectually safeguard our country against the inroads of disease, and at the same time not put the importer to such a
fMr Gardiner.]
very great expense as he is sometimes forced to incur. To give one illustration, some bauxite, the raw material for aluminum, was shipped to 'Canada in sacks from a country which I think was classed as infected, and the importer was forced to send the shipment back to Great Britain, I think it was, and .to have it resacked in new sacks, and brought out again. There was another case a few years ago which I mention just to illustrate my point; some cotton came in, wrapped in burlap, and a similar dispute arose. My suggestion to the minister is not that there should be relaxation of the necessary precautions, but that in such a case the importer might be permitted to repack the goods on the wharf, and the packings that came in could be destroyed; in other words, that some effort be made to minimize the loss to the importer, while at the same time adequately safeguarding the health of the animals of this country by preventing the inroads of disease from some other country. I believe that a good deal could be done along that line.

I can only say that there are countries which are ravaged by disease like foot and mouth disease, countries which if we had an outbreak of foot and mouth disease would probably put an embargo on our cattle for as many years as it was maintained at one time previously in our history. We must be very careful in connection with shipments that come in from a country so infected. A few shipments have come in, in second-hand gunny sacks which had been used for some other purpose before, in contravention of the well-known regulations. It has been considered advisable to have such shipments returned and not allowed to enter this country at all. The department is very exacting about that, and I do not know that it would pay us to remove any of these restrictions. We would be running the chance of suffering very great inconvenience ourselves in a very short time just to accommodate one or two individuals.

I think if the importer were put to the trouble and expense and delay of repacking .the goods and destroying the containers right on the wharf it would be a sufficient penalty to make him more careful next time; but a rigid enforcement of the law, compelling the importer to ship back the whole thing, might seriously affect business in other lines, and sometimes the shipment may have come in quite innocently so far as the importer is concerned. The exporter in a foreign country cannot possibly be as familiar with our regulations as the importer on this side, or know how exacting the department

Supply-Agriculture-Seed Control
is, and there are bound to be cases where there may seem to be a disregard of the regulations but where there was no intention of breaking them at all. I do submit that with a little cooperation the loss to the importer could be minimized and other lines of business not seriously injured, as they well might 'be by a rigid adherence to the regulations.

I am informed that there is a good deal of cooperation and that every case is considered on its merits. There are cases where the very thing my hon. friend suggests is being carried out, but there are other cases where conditions perhaps are such at the point where the goods came from that we do not want our own officials or anybody here to handle the commodity at all, and where it is returned for repacking. There is a great deal of risk taken in connection with such a shipment. The number of cases such as my hon. friend mentions must be very limited, but I shall be glad to take into consideration what he has said.
I have heard of a goodly number of such cases.
What progress has been made in the control of the corn borer in western Ontario?

There has been considerable improvement since the days when the farmers in that section were considering going out of growing corn because of the corn borer, but the greater part of that work is done by the provincial government. They ask for assistance from us through services that we can give through this branch, and that assistance is given in cooperation with them. But the main activity is carried on by the provincial government.

Can the minister tell us something about the control methods that have been adopted in regard to the pea moth? In the lower mainland of British Columbia there has been a considerable loss because of the depredations of the pea moth; in fact, they cannot grow peas at all in that section. I should like to know what is being done to control this pest.
Will the hon. member let his question stand until we reach item 30, dealing with entomology?
Do grasshoppers come under this vote?
No, under the entomology item.

Seed, feed and fertilizer control, including grant of $18,900 to Canadian Seed Growers' Association, $546,403.
Would the minister explain the increase of 838,396?

There is an increase in certain activities amounting to $58,396, and a decrease in others of $20,000, making a net increase of $38,396. Salaries for the permanent staff are increased by $19,801, and for the temporary staff, $29,595; subsidies and contributions, a decrease of $20,000; maintenance of buildings and lands, an increase of $1,800; professional and special services, an increase of $6,000; travelling expenses, an increase of $1,200.

A question was asked in the house not long ago as to what size of farm is the most profitable to operate. It entirely depends on the line of fanning you wish to follow, whether it be tobacco farming, fruit farming, mixed farming, and so forth. The farmer realizes that the farm is productive only to a certain degree, and that certain types of soil require certain kinds of fertilizer. I believe that provincially some help has been given, but I wonder what the dominion government has been doing along that line-speaking primarily now of Ontario and eastern Canada. I asked the bureau of statistics what the average production was of grains per acre in Ontario, and I learned that during the past twenty years the production was: barley, 29 bushels, oats, 36 bushels, and wheat, 23 bushels. I submit that if the right types of fertilizer were used that productivity could be increased, because in eastern Canada particularly we have abundance of rainfall; I believe we could almost double that yield. No matter what the production per acre, we have the same amount of taxes to pay on the land, and the same amount of work to do. In my opinion fertilizer should be provided at a reasonable cost, enabling the farmer to purchase it at a reasonable price. Very often the farmer has used his fertilizer without knowing just what type is required for his particular soil. I believe that at one time the department put in some mixing plants to make fertilizer available for the farmer at cost or nearly so.

I understand that that work so far as Ontario is concerned is being carried on through the provincial government, largely at the Guelph farm. Soils are sent in for analysis; it is determined what type of fertilizer should be used, and as a result the farmer can purchase the type he requires. It

is just possible that there are many farmers who do not take advantage of this service; also there may be many who do. Sometimes I go up to the western part of Ontario, and I find that some of the farmers there are having their lands tested continuously and the proper fertilizers placed upon them.

Certain criticisms have been levelled directly and indirectly against the department for changing the regulation during the past year with respect to the colouring of seed coming from Great Britain and New Zealand. I believe that that regulation, which had been in effect for some time, enabled the farmer to know whether he was buying imported seed or Canadian seed. There may be a good reason why the change was made last year, but I think the minister would be wise to let the committee know just what were the circumstances which led to that decision, because I have heard complaints about it.

I understand there was a change in the regulations which was intended to result in a different colouring being used for English seed from that used for seed from other countries. That was in effect for a short time; it was found to be unsatisfactory, and the present recommendation is to return to the old colouring and that all imported seed be coloured.

Did I understand the minister to say that there has been no seed imported from Great Britain and New Zealand which was not coloured? I understood that that regulation had been suspended in the meantime.

For one year prior to January 1 it was possible for the seed to come in without any colouring, and from January on this special colouring was adopted. Now it is recommended that we go back to the original regulation regarding staining.
What reason was assigned for that?
It was intended to be a courtesy to the British seed grower, but in practice it was found not to be practical. The desire was to give some consideration to the British seed grower.
I notice the minister said there was a reduction in grants. Would he give us some particulars of the reductions?

The subsidies and contributions show a decrease of $20,000. The amount was previously provided under this vote as a contribution to seed distribution
policies in western Canada. This work is now largely covered by the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, therefore the item for subsidies and contributions has been reduced accordingly.
It is really a removal, not a reduction?
Yes. There is much more than that being spent under the rehabilitation policy.

What is the reason for the grant to the Saskatoon winter fair being $9,500, while to the Edmonton winter fair it is only $5,000? That appears on page 64. Why this great difference between Saskatoon and Edmonton?

Item agreed to.
Experimental farms-Experimental farms administration, $51,180.

The other day I asked a question which the minister said could be better discussed under experimental farms. I understand that a number of graduates in Saskatchewan holding various degrees from western universities are employed in the soil surveys work and for several years have been paid on the basis of fifty-five cents an hour as graduate labourers. These men are doing very important work, and some of them are now getting into the thirties and still doing this work as graduate labourers. Are men who come within this category going to receive some consideration this year? In common with other members of the house, not only western members, but generally, we regard
the survey of these western soils as of paramount importance to the dominion. In fact, it is unfortunate that the surveys were not undertaken years ago. Saskatchewan has done a great deal with the small appropriations available, and it seems to me that this work should be extended to cover the entire western area so that we may be prepared when we come to rehabilitate the country, as ultimately we shall have to do, because I have disquieting news from parts of Saskatchewan where there were copious rains. Some consideration should be given this particular staff, especially those of the university of Saskatchewan.

These men were previously working on the fifty-five cents an hour paylist, but their positions have been classified under the reorganization, and as they qualify through length of service and the necessity for their work is realized they will come under that classification. Some are already under it.

I am glad to know that.
I was not aware that the reclassification had taken place.
The salary of the director of experimental farms is $7,500. Last year it was $6,000. Is there any reason for the increase? The minister will find the details on page 64.
The actual increase is only $500. Previously $1,000 was paid out of another service, which made his salary $7,000. Now it is $7,500.

Last year,
according to the estimates, his salary was $6,000, and from now on it will be $7,500.

It will all appear in one vote now. As a matter of fact, he was receiving $7,000 last year, though the salary for the position of director was $6,000. He obtained another $1,000 from another source, so that his salary was actually $7,000. Now it is being consolidated and there is an increase of $500.

Last year and this year again I raised the question of labourers' wages on experimental farms. I understand that the rate of pay was increased for seasonal workers from twenty-one to twenty-five cents an hour, which was something. Many of these men are married and they work only a few months, so that they find it difficult to make sufficient in the summer to carry them through the winter. Moreover, I have been given to understand that conditions on the Scott experimental farm in regard to boarding houses and so on require the attention of the inspectors. I do not know whether complaints of that kind are justified, but recently I received a letter asking me to bring the matter

to the attention of the minister. I was going to do so by letter, but the opportunity has arisen this afternoon and I am mentioning the matter. With regard to these men who are working on the farms, the seasonal workers, some further consideration should be given them especially, as was pointed out by an hon. member sitting to my right, in view of the fact that large increases are given sometimes to heads of departments, increases that might well be distributed among the more poorly paid workers. If the conditions at some of the experimental farms in regard to boarding places require inspection, I suggest that the matter might be checked up.

Of course, complaints
do come in occasionally with regard to conditions in boarding houses in connection with all activities, and we receive such complaints in connection with the farms. The conditions are always investigated as soon as possible after the complaints are received and are dealt with. So far as labour on the farms is concerned, there are two sides to the question. We try to pay a reasonable wage, but sometimes we come into conflict with those who are engaging agricultural assistants in the community and who consider that we overpay. We try to strike a happy medium and pay a reasonable rate without doing any injury in the district itself.
What happens to produce grown on the experimental farms?

A great deal of what is produced is used experimentally. Some of it is fed on the farms, and some commodity such as milk is sold in some communities. We try to sell it in such a way as not to create competition with persons engaged in private industry.
There must be a vast quantity of vegetables grown on the experimental farms, more than can be used on the farm itself. Is it given away to charitable organizations, or is it sold?

Some of the vegetables are grown for storage tests and those, of course, are put in storage. Many of the vegetables grown are of so many types and varieties that there is no sale for them in bulk. They are fed, if there is stock to consume them, or they are disposed of in some other way. There is no general policy, there being no sale for them.

We have an experimental farm in Ottawa, and undoubtedly they must grow a vast quantity of vegetables of all sorts. There are many people in the city without gardens who could possibly use that 
surplus. I am not referring to anything of value for experimental purposes, but the surplus that is not used could be distributed to those who have not gardens of their own and who would appreciate a supply of fresh vegetables in the winter. I think it would be a nice gesture for the department to offer to give these surplus vegetables to poor people, until the supply is exhausted.

There is really only one way in which that could be done without difficulty; that is, to give it to hospitals, or to the Red Cross or the Salvation Army or such organizations to distribute. It would be very difficult for the farmers to distribute it themselves, and decide who is entitled and who is not. The wholesalers take anything that is of value.
Is there some revenue from the sale of pure bred breeding stock?
Yes; there is a certain revenue.

I referred a moment ago to
the experiments with landrace hogs. Last year we had some startling figures placed on Hansard) by the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair). They seemed to indicate that the early maturing quality of these hogs in comparison with other types experimented with at the farm is almost incredible. Could the minister tell us briefly what experiments have been carried on during the past year and the results in relation to early maturity, and their adaptability for bacon?

The results of the experiments carried on to date have been given publicity through the press. A complete statement has been put out. I have not the report before me at the moment or I would read it. Generally speaking, the results show that there are some advantages in the type of hog that was introduced, and some disadvantages. From the experiments to date, it is not considered that there is sufficient balance of advantages over disadvantages to warrant attempting to interfere with the type we now have pretty well established across Canada, the Yorkshire type.

Would the minister give a statement concerning the experiments carried out at Indian Head and other stations in Saskatchewan with respect to rust resisting wheat, and when we may expect to have a general distribution of the varieties being experimented with during the last year?

Item agreed to.
Central experimental farm, Ottawa, $594,135.

As a result of the
experiments carried on at Indian Head in connection with rust resistant wheats, there are three unnamed varieties now being carried under numbers. If they prove entirely successful, they will be distributed. There has been some distribution this last year of Thatcher wheat and Renown as well. But these other three varieties being developed we hope will be even better than those which have been distributed.

Would it not
be possible, either in the supplementaries or in next year's estimates, to provide for building at least one more large greenhouse at the experimental farm for the purpose of carrying on this work with rust resistant wheat and oats, and also experiments with beans, peas and other plants used in every part of Canada? Some ten years ago the greenhouses were enlarged, and the result has been a tremendous amount of good work done in building up new and better grains for Canada, especially rust resistant varieties. More greenhouse accommodation would not involve a very great expenditure. The department and the men who handle these grains should be highly complimented upon the work they have done. I have heard in the committee criticisms of the salaries paid to men in the experimental farms, but I believe most of these men are not paid enough. If we were to pay more money in these positions, we might have held some of the good men we have lost and be able to keep some of the good men who are coming along. There is no more useful work in connection with agriculture in this country. I hope the minister will soon be able to provide a sufficient sum to give these people more room to work.

The work being done
by the experimental farms is recognized throughout western Canada as being of a very high order. I wish to add my commendation and that of this group to what has been said. The development of Thatcher
wheat and so on has done much for western Canada, and that work is appreciated by the farmers. Anything that can be done to assist the biologists and botanists who are carrying on this work should be done. We know the work cannot be done without greenhouses and equipment.
